slides.title: Wiki Memory in a Database Can I put
slides.text: Wiki Memory in a Database Can I put a wiki memory into a database? MongoDB or PostgreSQL? Will I be able to reproduce the speed and quality of the local search? How local search works: a python script does an exact substring or regex scan, then sort by match count with a title bonus. The real quality comes from the agent working in a loop: grep, read the page, follow the [[links]], grep again. A database keeps that quality as long as it offers the same four operations with the same exact-match behavior. Both PostgreSQL and MongoDB can store wiki pages, metadata, and links. Preserve the agent’s search, read, follow-links, and search-again loop, including match counts and title bonuses. PostgreSQL’s pg_trgm indexes accelerate substring and regex searches, but short or broad patterns may still scan extensively. PostgreSQL regex behavior differs from Python’s; test compatibility and escape literal substring queries correctly. Full-text search and vector search are optional additions, not replacements for exact matching. Store links in a relationship table and flexible metadata in jsonb. Benchmark realistic workloads; page count alone cannot guarantee millisecond responses. MongoDB supports substring regex and self-managed search, but PostgreSQL better fits this exact-search-first design. Andrej Karpathy has popularized the idea of using obsidian wiki as agentic memory in April of 2026 Idea - preserve original sources, let an LLM maintain interlinked Markdown pages, and use instruction files to govern updates, organization, and consistency Agents ingest sources, answer questions, and check the wiki for contradictions, outdated information, and missing connections Knowledge accumulates as persistent, human-readable memory rather than being rebuilt for every query https://gist.github.com/karpathy/442a6bf555914893e9891c11519de94f https://aaif.io/blog/karpathys-llm-wiki-as-agent-memory

slides.title: South African AI-novelist Coral Hart South African AI-novelist
slides.text: South African AI-novelist Coral Hart South African AI-novelist Coral Hart says she has published 371 books, many of them romance novels, using AI since February 2025. She develops the concepts, characters, style, and chapter outlines, then uses tools including ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok to generate and revise the text. A human proofreader checks and rewrites portions before publication . Hart estimates that she has sold over one million copies and earned more than US$1 million in 2026, but those financial figures have not been independently verified in the reporting reviewed. The viral post’s claim that a finished book takes just 45 minutes She sells through Amazon, at least: reporting on Coral Hart says one of her novels reached an Amazon top-100 bestseller list Her reported sales span e-books, print books, and audiobooks, but the sources do not provide a complete list of retailers or audiobook platforms. I could not confirm Kobo, Apple Books, Audible, or other specific stores She publishes under more than ten other pen names, so searching only for “Coral Hart” would not reveal her full catalogue The million-copy sales figure is her own estimate across formats—not a verified Amazon-only sales total

slides.title: AI News OpenAI and Anthropic claim the Exponential
slides.text: AI News OpenAI and Anthropic claim the Exponential Time Hypothesis is false The Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH) is a hypothesis in computational complexity stating that solving certain problems requires exponential time in the worst case OpenAI posted a preprint and a Lean-verified proof that ETH fails Anthropic published a parallel refutation credited to Claude ETH has been assumed for about 30 years; hundreds of papers rely on it Not peer reviewed yet; OpenAI says it gives no practical SAT algorithm https://www.webpronews.com/openai-anthropic-exponential-time-hypothesis-refuted-sat Axiom machine-checks the longest proof in mathematics Complete Lean formalization of the Classification of Finite Simple Groups Original proof: about 15,000 pages in 500+ papers by 100+ mathematicians Agent swarms wrote about 43 million lines of Lean in 24 days Agents claimed tasks, reviewed each other and merged through GitHub, with human guidance Fixed hundreds of errata in the published proof Now the largest computer-verified proof, past the four-color theorem https://axiommath.ai/research/the-enormous-theorem-formalized/ Claude proves 123 open-source libraries never crash Anthropic and Theorem covered 239 fuzz entry points in 123 OSS-Fuzz libraries About 180 million lines of Rocq proofs, checked by the Rocq kernel Claim: no crash for any input under 64 MB Claude turned each fuzz test into a spec, then wrote the proof Found and patched bugs that fuzzing had missed Limits: single-threaded static RISC-V binaries on Linux with musl https://interestingengineering.com/ai-robotics/claude-formal-verification-software-security

slides.title: AI News Liquid AI LFM3: open on-device models
slides.text: AI News Liquid AI LFM3: open on-device models from 1.7B Text, vision, audio, omni and decision models on one tri-hybrid backbone The 1.7B text model beats its 2.6B predecessor with 35% fewer parameters Beats Qwen3.5-9B in some tests! Fits in about 1 GB at 4-bit with a 256K context window LFM3-VL-2B adds video input and matches Gemma 4 12B on 62 vision benchmarks Every model fine-tunes on a single GPU Aimed at browser automation, voice and vision agents on local hardware https://www.liquid.ai/blog/lfm3 Phonon: a 31M-parameter text-to-speech model, now in Ollama Gradium, spun out of Kyutai, open-sourced Phonon 31m under Apache 2.0 First audio in 6.9 ms on a MacBook Air M5 CPU, against 517 ms for Kokoro 1.70% WER on hard sentences with phone numbers and emails Runs 3.7x faster than real time on a Raspberry Pi 5 Ollama 0.40.11 adds speech: ollama run phonon "Hello" Only the English 31m model is commercial; others are CC BY-NC https://ollama.com/blog/speech-models OpenAI’s Claimed Science Advances Disproved the Exponential Time Hypothesis, challenging assumed computational limits; the proof was formalized in Lean. Math claims include local smoothing and Kakeya conjectures across all dimensions; physics claims include quantum chromodynamics and Yang–Mills existence, not the complete Millennium Prize problem https://openai.com/index/building-scientific-understanding-with-academic-communities/
